cross_cutting.description: Cloudflare's first open-source decision models, now on Workers AI ... Meet@cf/cloudflare/clef and @cf/cloudflare/clef-flash, the first models trained by the Cloudflare Workers AI team, available on Workers AI today.
cross_cutting.content:
# Introducing Clef: Cloudflare's first open-source decision models, now on Workers AI
import { TypeScriptExample } from "~/components";

Meet@cf/cloudflare/clef and @cf/cloudflare/clef-flash, the first models trained by the Cloudflare Workers AI team, available on Workers AI today.

Clef is a decision model, in the same family as Typesafe's Jev. Instead of generating text, it reads an input state and a set of typed questions, then returns a probability for every allowed answer. Your agent gets a structured decision it can act on immediately, for example: route the ticket, block the request, or escalate to a human. There is no free-form output to parse and no reasoning tokens to wait for.

Both models are hosted on Workers AI as Clef and Clef-flash. We are also open-sourcing the weights under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face: Clef and Clef-flash. Read the launch blog post for the full story, including how we trained them.

We are also launching a reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning service to help you tune Clef for your own workloads. Sign up to work with us as a design partner.

## Built for the hot path

Clef is designed to be fast so decisions come back in milliseconds. Across our 43 benchmark runs, we achieved speeds where Clef is 2.5x faster than Jev at the median, and Clef-flash 13x faster.

Latency | Clef | Clef-flash | Jev 
---|---|---|---
Median | 209.3 ms | 38.8 ms | 524.1 ms 
p95 | 238.6 ms | 122.4 ms | 536.0 ms 

Hosting on Workers AI adds to that speed. Requests run on GPUs across Cloudflare's network, running close to your users, so the network round trip stays short. You can put Clef directly in the request path of your agent, then hand off to an LLM on Workers AI to take action.

## Leading the benchmarks

Across 10 decision benchmarks, a Clef model scores highest on 7, ahead of Jev and other open decision models. A few highlights:

Benchmark | Clef | Clef-flash | Jev 
---|---|---|---
BFCL (case exact) | 98.47 | 98.76 | 95.75 
BANKING77 (macro-F1) | 94.20 | 90.93 | 79.74 
CLINC150+OOS (macro-F1) | 97.43 | 66.77 | 89.27 
Home appliances (case exact) | 82.95 | 97.73 | 52.27 

On Typesafe's own workflow evals, Clef beats Jev in 3 of 4 areas: invoice processing, customer service, and security incidents. The full results are on the Hugging Face model card.

## Drop-in compatible with Jev

Model | Size | Best for | Context window 
---|---|---|---
@cf/cloudflare/clef27B | Highest-precision decisions | 64K tokens 
@cf/cloudflare/clef-flash9B | Latency-critical, hot-path decisions | 64K tokens 

Clef follows the System One API, so you can switch an existing Jev integration to Clef by changing the endpoint and model. Ask up to 64 questions per request, in three types:

- noul: A yes/no question. Returns the probability that the answer is yes.
- choice: Pick one option from a set you define. Returns the chosen option, a probability per option, and a confidence value.
- score: Rate against an ordered rubric. Returns a probability-weighted score and a probability per level.

const response = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clef", {
	model: "clef",
	state: "Checkout has been failing for every customer for the last hour.",
	questions: {
		urgent: {
			type: "noul",
			instructions: "Is this support request urgent?",
		},
		team: {
			type: "choice",
			instructions: "Which team should handle this request?",
			criteria: {
				billing: "Payments, invoices, and refunds",
				technical: "Outages, errors, and configuration",
				sales: "Plans and upgrades",
			},
		},
	},
});

// response.answers.urgent.noul -> probability the request is urgent
// response.answers.team.choice -> highest-probability team

## What you can build with decision models

- Support triage: Decide whether a ticket is urgent and which team owns it, then route it without a human in the loop.
- Threat intelligence: Classify a website by category. Paired with Browser Run, Clef fetched, rendered, and classified a domain in 2.2 seconds, compared to 4.7 seconds forgpt-oss-120b in the same workflow.
- Trust and safety: Score user submissions against your own policy rubric and act on the probability.
- Agent guardrails: Let an agent check "should I take this action?" in tens of milliseconds before calling a tool.
- Visual classification: Pass up to four images alongside the state. Unlike text-only decision models, Clef has a vision encoder.

## Get started

Use Clef through the Workers AI binding (env.AI.run()) or the REST API at /ai/run. You can also use AI Gateway with these endpoints.

For more information, refer to the Clef model page, the Clef-flash model page, and pricing.

# Sarvam's new AI model promises better performance at lower cost

## Sarvam’s latest model promises better reasoning, tool use and Indian-language capabilities at lower costs, as competition to build India’s AI ecosystem gathers pace.

Monday November 23, 2026 , 3 min Read

Sarvam AI has released Sarvam-105B-1711, an updated model designed for businesses handling large volumes of customer queries, phone calls and software-based tasks. The company said it follows instructions more reliably, uses digital tools better and handles Indian languages more effectively, at a lower cost.

Released on November 22, it updates Sarvam’s 105B model, first released in March. The 105 billion parameters refers to the internal values the model adjusts during training to recognise patterns and produce answers.

Sarvam said it trained the new version using Nvidia’s Blackwell B200 chips, powerful processors built for AI calculations.

Co-founder Pratyush Kumar said, “Over the last few months, alongside putting together the token factory and scaling up our enterprise offerings, we optimised our training stack for Blackwell GPUs and achieved significantly higher performance.”

The training stack refers to the hardware, software and processes used to train the model.

Sarvam described it as a “Flash-Lite” model, meaning it is designed to handle many requests at relatively low cost. Its architecture activates only selected parts of the model to generate each response, helping reduce computing requirements. Potential uses include customer-service chatbots, AI voice assistants that speak with callers, and digital assistants that use other software to complete tasks.

Sarvam is making the model’s learned settings, known as weights, available for download. This is called an open-weight release. It allows businesses with suitable computers to run the model themselves rather than relying entirely on Sarvam’s online service. The company has also published instructions for running and training it, although the data used to train the model are not necessarily public.

Sarvam said the new version scored 73.9 on average across eight tests, compared with 42.6 for its March model. The tests assess how well it follows instructions, writes responses, uses software tools and handles Indian languages. These are average scores, not percentages of questions answered correctly. Sarvam’s comparison places it close to Google’s Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, at 74.0, and Gemma 4 31B, at 73.0.

Cost is central to the release. Sarvam noted the combined cost of processing text sent to and generated by the model has fallen from $0.44 to $0.15 per million tokens. Tokens are small pieces of text, sometimes whole words and sometimes parts of words, that an AI model reads or produces. Its Indian rates are Rs 10 per million input tokens and Rs 25 per million output tokens.

The latest release is part of a broader push by Sarvam to build models for different AI applications. Earlier in November, the company introduced Sarvam Prism, a model built on its 105B system for making quick, straightforward decisions. It also released Bulbul V4 Flash in October, which converts written text into natural-sounding speech, and Saaras V4 in September, which converts spoken language into text across 22 Indian languages.

Other Indian companies are pursuing similar ambitions, although their models target different needs. In August, Bengaluru-based Gnani AI introduced Evon v3.3, a 30-billion-parameter model designed to work across 11 Indian languages, alongside Plexus, a platform for building AI assistants that can perform tasks.

More recently, under the IndiaAI Mission, Soket Labs introduced EKA-1, a 26.3-billion-parameter model designed for all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English, with applications in mathematics, coding and reasoning.

# Changelog

All notable changes to AbstractCore will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

Unreleased changes live inchangelog.d/, one file per pull request;
python scripts/changelog.py assemble X.Y.Z writes them here at release.

## [Unreleased]

## [2.37.0] - 2026-11-23

### Added

- Thinking Machines Inkling family in the capability registry (assets/model_capabilities.json,
assets/architecture_formats.json). Inkling 2 Mini, Inkling 2 Small, Inkling and Inkling Small resolve to
their entries (inkling-2-mini-26b-a3b, inkling-2-small-594b-a17b, inkling-975b-a41b,
inkling-small-276b-a12b) from the plain names (inkling-2-mini, inkling, ...), the published repository
names (thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini, thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Small-MXFP8,
thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4, ...) and GGUF or MLX re-packagings, and to the new inkling architecture.
Tool calling is native, so OpenAI-compatible servers running vLLM or SGLang with --tool-call-parser inkling
receive the tools in the request's tools field and return parsed tool_calls. Reasoning arrives in
message.reasoning. thinking maps to reasoning_effort: minimal, low, medium and high on every
model, plus xhigh on Inkling 2; thinking="off" sends the lowest effort, because no Inkling effort value
turns reasoning off. Entries declare a 1,048,576-token context, image input (and voice and sound input on
Inkling and Inkling Small), and max_output_tokens 32,768. An Inkling release the registry does not list yet
(thinkingmachines/Inkling-3-...) gets native tool calling from the architecture, and a model whose name only
contains the word (twinkling-7b) is not read as an Inkling model.
- nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4-QAD is an alias of qwen3.8-27b (assets/model_capabilities.json), so
NVIDIA's quantization-aware-distilled NVFP4 build resolves to the registered model by name.
- Chunks that carry the pieces of a native tool call are marked withchunk.metadata["tool_call_delta"] = True (OpenAI-compatible, OpenAI and Anthropic streams). You can use it
to show that a call is on its way; time to first token counts the first marked chunk.

### Changed

- A native tool call the model did not finish is reported, not delivered (providers/native_tool_calls.py,
providers/base.py). When a model stops in the middle of a call, usually at max_output_tokens
(finish_reason: "length"), its arguments are not a JSON object. Such a call used to come back as a tool
call with empty arguments ({}), which an agent could execute. It is now left out of tool_calls, streamed
or not, and reported in metadata["unparsed_tool_call"] (format: "native", everything the model wrote, and
reason: "unclosed" or "unparseable") with metadata["tool_call_error"] and a warning, the same way an
unparsed text tool call is reported. A call without arguments ("", null or {}) is delivered as before.

### Fixed

Troubleshooting covers announced but missing tool calls (
docs/troubleshooting.md). When a server
reports a model under a name the registry does not know, tools are sent in prompted mode, and servers that parse
tool calls per model (vLLM or SGLang --tool-call-parser) return no call. The guide shows how to check the
resolved tool_support and how to fix it.

Streamed native tool calls arrive complete (
providers/native_tool_calls.py,
providers/openai_compatible_provider.py, providers/openai_provider.py,
providers/anthropic_provider.py). With stream=True, OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible servers (vLLM, LM Studio,

- OpenAI-compatible and OpenAI streams join the fragments by index and deliver the calls on the chunk that carries thefinish_reason, as {"id", "type", "name", "arguments": "<JSON string>"}; parallel calls
arrive together and in order, and an OpenAI-compatible stream that ends without a finish reason still
delivers its calls on a last chunk.

- OpenAI streams no longer repeat, on the chunk that carries the calls, the text already streamed in that turn.

A streamed call carries the same name and argument values as the non-streamed one. If you assembled
delta.tool_calls fragments from chunk.tool_calls yourself, use the complete call, or read the raw deltas
from chunk.raw_response.

# Levenza launches personal AI agents for enterprise
Tue, 24th Nov 2026 (Today) 
SOFIAH NICHOLE SALIVIO News Editor

Levenza has launched its personal AI agents globally for enterprise customers and acquired voice AI lab Fluid Inference, extending the San Francisco company's offering as it seeks wider adoption among large professional services firms.

Its software is already used by more than 300 customers, including Oliver Wyman, Goodwin and Hg Capital. The company says it has also signed multiple million-dollar contracts and grown profitably without outside capital.

The agents work inside Teams, Slack and Outlook, handling administrative tasks such as scheduling meetings, booking rooms, liaising with travel agents and submitting timesheets. The software also manages to-do lists by picking up commitments from meetings, chats and email, then working through open tasks in the background.

The acquisition of Fluid Inference adds voice interaction. Users can now speak to their agents while commuting or away from their desks to get a briefing on the day ahead, work through urgent emails and rearrange meetings.

Fluid Inference was acquired in September, and its founder, Brandon Weng, has joined Levenza as Head of Engineering. The lab develops open-source models for speech and multimodal AI, including FluidAudio, and says its speech and system one models have been downloaded more than 4.7 million times and are used in more than 60 apps.

Levenza is targeting a part of the office software market where employers are looking for measurable returns from AI spending. Administrative work, especially around calendars, internal coordination and follow-up tasks, has become a frequent target for automation as companies look beyond experimental deployments.

Enterprise settings are harder to navigate than consumer use, the company argues, because calendars shift constantly, hierarchy affects whose time takes priority and many requests pass through executive assistants. Levenza says it adapts its software to each customer's internal processes through engineers who work directly with clients.

That has made consulting, law and investment firms a core market. Its customer list also includes Kearney, Baird and Spencer Stuart.

"People have seen what personal AI agents can do outside work, and they're expecting the same experience in the office," said Haefa Mansour, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Levenza. "But most people at work are still spending hours every week coordinating schedules, chasing replies and tracking tasks. We built Levenza to take responsibility for that work."

The business was founded two and a half years ago by Mansour, a former Bain consultant with a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley, and Austin Tackaberry, a former engineer at Databricks and Uber. It has expanded through customer revenue and word of mouth rather than venture funding.

Customer growth

Customers often increase their use after signing up, according to the company. It reported net revenue retention of 170% and gross revenue retention of 99%, figures that suggest existing clients are renewing and spending more over time.

The company also says more than 95% of professionals using its product rate it highly, while some users report feeling less stressed at work. The claims come as software suppliers race to show that AI tools can save time on routine work rather than simply generate content.

Goodwin is among the firms using the product. "I've used several AI scheduling tools and Levenza stands out, as it's the first AI scheduling tool that fits how I already work," said Dustin Finer, Managing Director of Administration at Goodwin. "It handles quick one-on-ones and more complex meetings with ease, coordinating across calendars and time zones seamlessly. Plus, Levenza lives in our existing environment, so there was no new platform to adopt."

Wider market

Levenza's launch comes as the market for personal AI agents gains attention in both consumer and workplace software. Consumer products have driven much of the early interest, but enterprise adoption has moved more slowly because of integration demands, security concerns and the complexity of internal workflows.

The company also pointed to broader pressure on corporate technology teams to prove returns from AI investments. It cited a Gartner survey of more than 2,000 Chief Information Officers in which 13% said their organisations had realised significant value from AI, as well as Microsoft research showing workers face heavy email volumes and frequent interruptions.

Levenza plans to expand the range of tasks its agents can take on, with travel booking and expense management due in 2027. For now, its pitch rests on a narrower claim: handling routine administrative work is one of the clearest areas where AI can show immediate value inside large organisations.

# Levenza launches personal AI agents globally for the enterprise

Levenza is bringing consumer-style personal agents into the enterprise. Already used by more than 300 customers, including Oliver Wyman, Goodwin and Hg Capital, the company has grown quickly and profitably without raising outside capital.

Personal AI agents have become this year’s biggest breakthrough in consumer technology. Levenza is bringing them to the enterprise.

The company announced the global availability of its AI agents, alongside its acquisition of Fluid Inference. Fluid Inference is an applied AI lab focused on ambient intelligence.

Operating inside Teams, Slack and Outlook, Levenza’s agents proactively manage admin work. This includes complex scheduling coordination, booking rooms, liaising with travel agents and submitting timesheets. They also run each person’s to-do list. They pick up commitments from meetings, chats and email and work through open tasks in the background.

Over time, they learn each person’s preferences. The acquisition adds voice, allowing people to speak to their agents while commuting or away from their desks.

“People have seen what personal AI agents can do outside work, and they’re expecting the same experience in the office,” said Haefa Mansour, Co-Founder and CEO of Levenza. “But most people at work are still spending hours every week coordinating schedules, chasing replies and tracking tasks. We built Levenza to take responsibility for that work.”

## Substantial traction

The launch comes with substantial traction. Levenza has signed over 300 customers, including Oliver Wyman, Kearney, Goodwin, Baird, Hg Capital and Spencer Stuart. It has secured multiple million-dollar enterprise contracts and grown profitably without raising outside capital.

Customers keep expanding after they sign: Levenza’s net revenue retention is 170%, and its gross revenue retention is 99%. More than 95% of professionals using Levenza rate it highly, and many report feeling happier and less stressed at work.

“I’ve used several AI scheduling tools and Levenza stands out, as it’s the first AI scheduling tool that fits how I already work,” said Dustin Finer, Managing Director of Administration at Goodwin. “It handles quick one-on-ones and more complex meetings with ease, coordinating across calendars and time zones seamlessly. Plus, Levenza lives in our existing environment, so there was no new platform to adopt.”

## Acquiring Fluid Inference

Levenza acquired Fluid Inference in September to accelerate its vision of an AI agent that people can talk to as naturally as another person. The research lab builds open-source models that hear, see, decide and speak, including FluidAudio, a #1 trending GitHub project.

Its speech and system one models have been downloaded more than 4.7 million times. They are used in more than 60 apps, including FluidVoice, VoiceInk and Spokenly. Fluid Inference was also a launch partner for NVIDIA’s Nemotron speech models. It has worked with Intel to bring speech and language models to AI PCs. Its founder, Brandon Weng, has joined Levenza as Head of Engineering.

The companies have already integrated voice into Levenza’s platform. Someone driving to work can call their agent for a briefing on the day ahead, work through urgent emails and rearrange meetings without opening a laptop.

Users can also dictate directly into applications. Voice is part of a broader ambition to make interacting with enterprise software less dependent on navigating applications and typing instructions.

## Bringing personal agents into the enterprise

While consumer agents have demonstrated how powerful personal AI can be, enterprise environments are considerably more complex. Calendars are busy and constantly changing, hierarchies decide whose time comes first and many requests route through executive assistants.

Levenza is built for that complexity. Its forward-deployed engineers work directly with customers to adapt the agent to how each firm operates. A professional can ask Levenza in Teams or Slack to arrange a client meeting and have it inspect calendars, coordinate with assistants, resolve conflicts and book the time.

Levenza serves professionals without dedicated administrative support and the executive assistants already carrying the most complex workloads. Users report saving up to three hours a day. Travel booking and expenses launch in 2027, widening the amount of admin work professionals can hand over.

## The founding journey

Levenza was born from Mansour’s experience working long hours at Bain. There, she saw firsthand how much time professionals and executive assistants lost to routine coordination. A UC Berkeley PhD, she founded the company two and a half years ago with Austin Tackaberry, a former Databricks and Uber engineer.

The company has remained largely under the radar, growing through enterprise word of mouth with almost no marketing to date. While the AI industry has attracted enormous amounts of venture funding, Levenza has financed its growth through customer revenue. It built a profitable business before its broader market launch.

## Looking ahead

The launch comes as companies face growing pressure to demonstrate measurable returns from their AI investments. An October Gartner survey of more than 2,000 CIOs found that just 13% said their organizations had realized significant value from AI.

Meanwhile, Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index found that the average worker receives 117 emails per day, faces interruptions every two minutes and increasingly coordinates meetings across time zones.

Levenza sees administrative work as one of the clearest opportunities for AI agents to deliver an immediate return. The company’s longer-term ambition goes beyond handling individual requests. Levenza is building out a network of agents that integrate deeply with enterprise systems and take ownership of high-level objectives.

The ultimate vision is a workplace where every professional has access to a personal agent. Executive assistants can focus more of their time on the strategic work that requires their judgment and relationships.

Consumer agents have shown what happens when AI starts acting on people’s behalf. Levenza is betting the next major opportunity is bringing that same experience to hundreds of millions of people at work.

## About Levenza

Levenza builds personal AI agents that handle administrative work for the enterprise, including scheduling, email, and room and venue booking, with expenses and travel booking launching in 2027.

For more information, please visit https://levenza.com/

### Bootstrapped startup Levenza brings consumer-style personal agents to business workers

Artificial intelligence enthusiasts are embracing personal agents that can automate life’s most tedious digital chores, but office workers are still stuck juggling calendars, email messages and chat threads.

Levenza wants to change that with the launch of what it says are the first personal AI agents designed for corporate employees. The startup today announced the general availability of its enterprise-grade personal agents, together with its first acquisition in the shape of the AI research lab Fluid Inference.

In the last few months, personal AI agents have emerged as the hottest new trend in AI, sparking fierce competition among both technology giants and agentic startups. The biggest name is probably Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse, a “secure by design” personal assistant that quickly shot to the top of U.S. app charts following its launch in September. We’ve also seen OpenAI’s Dots, powered by GPT-6 Astra, which aim to proactively get work done on behalf of their users, as well as startups such as Instinct, which raised a colossal $1 billion in funding in September for its consumer-focused agents.

AI agents may still be somewhat divisive, but the early success of Muse, Dots and Instinct shows that there’s clearly a large market for automated assistants. Yet those tools are all targeted primarily at consumers rather than enterprise workers, which means there’s a massive gap in the market that’s waiting to be filled. Levenza wants to be the one that fills it, with its personal agents developed specifically to run inside sensitive corporate environments.

### Personal agents built for work

Co-founder and Chief Executive Haefa Mansour (pictured, left) told SiliconANGLE that the difference between Levenza’s agents and those of its competitors is that it takes time to work with individual companies to customize what they can and can’t do. She explained that workplace agents can only provide value if they’re able to connect to corporate systems securely and respect a company’s dynamics and security policies.

“People have seen what personal AI agents can do outside of work, and they’re expecting the same experience inside the office,” Mansour said. “But most people at work are still spending hours every week coordinating schedules, cha50sing replies and tracking tasks. We built Levenza to take responsibility for that work.”

Levenza’s personal agents are designed to live inside of the platforms where work gets done, such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Slack. Within those environments, they act as proactive digital assistants for senior executives and other professionals.

Among other things, they can coordinate meetings across time zones, book hotel rooms, liaise with travel agencies, submit timesheets, triage overflowing email inboxes and send out replies and follow-ups when necessary. The more they do this work, the more they learn about the individual worker they’re serving, allowing them to become more useful over time, Mansour said.

By automating and coordinating routine work, Levenza’s agents can free workers from the “administrative drag” that affects every worker, slowing down productivity. “Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index found that the average worker receives 117 emails per day and is interrupted every two minutes,” Mansour said. “On top of the inbox and the calendar come the travel, expenses and follow-ups that slip through the cracks – none of this is work that professionals were actually hired to do.”

Mansour, a former Bain & Co. alumni who holds a Ph.D. from the University of California, founded Levenza alongside former Databricks Inc. and Uber Technologies Inc. engineer Austin Tackaberry (right) specifically to eliminate these distractions. The startup has made impressive traction, and despite not raising a dime in outside funding, its personal agents are already up and running at more than 300 enterprise customers, serving more than 10,000 professionals at those customers.

Early adopters such as Hg Capital and Oliver Wyman LLC report that their employees are saving up to three hours daily by offloading mundane admin to Levenza’s personal agents. They can also deal with any problems that occur during someone’s day. “For instance, if a manager’s customer workshop is running late and they’re likely to miss their flight, they don’t need to worry,” Mansour said. “Levenza will reach out to the travel management company to rebook according to their updated schedule.”

This means the manager in question will be able to focus on the workshop, safe in the knowledge that they’ll still be able to get to where they need to go after it does finish.

### Fluid Inference

The acquisition of Fluid Inference is all about making Levenza’s agents more accessible. Mansour said the startup is an open-source research lab that’s focused on developing AI speech and ambient intelligence models.

By buying it, Levenza will be able to integrate natural voice interactions with its agents, so workers won’t have to tell them what needs to be done. Fluid Inference’s founder Brandon Weng is going to stick around as Levenza’s new head of engineering, adding much-needed talent to its team.

With Levenza’s agents now generally available, Mansour says the company will use its growing revenues to expand its third-party integrations and develop more capabilities for them. The company plans to launch automations for travel booking and expense management early next year, but that’s just the beginning.

“In the future, Levenza agents will operate with full autonomy in the enterprise, proactively deciding what work needs to be done,” she said. “They’ll coordinate with groups of other Levenza agents to collectively accomplish tasks.”

##### Levenza runs scheduling, inbox, timesheets, and other administrative work inside Outlook, Teams, Slack, and Zoom, by text or voice. Levenza serves the world’s largest consulting and professional services firms, financial services firms, and Fortune 500 enterprises. Customers include Oliver Wyman, Goodwin, Baird, Kearney, Spencer Stuart, and Hg Capital.

San Francisco, CA, Nov. 23, 2026
(GLOBE NEWSWIRE)
-- Personal AI agents have become this year's biggest breakthrough in consumer technology.
Levenza
is bringing them to the enterprise.

Today, the company announced the global availability of its AI agents, alongside its acquisition of Fluid Inference, an applied AI lab focused on ambient intelligence. Operating inside Teams, Slack and Outlook, Levenza's agents proactively manage admin work, including complex scheduling coordination, booking rooms, liaising with travel agents and submitting timesheets. They also run each person’s to-do list, picking up commitments from meetings, chats and email and working through open tasks in the background. The acquisition adds voice, allowing people to speak to their agents while commuting or away from their desks.

Levenza founders Haefa Mansour and Austin Tackaberry.

"People have seen what personal AI agents can do outside work, and they're expecting the same experience in the office," said Haefa Mansour, Co-Founder and CEO of Levenza. "But most people at work are still spending hours every week coordinating schedules, chasing replies and tracking tasks. We built Levenza to take responsibility for that work.”

The launch comes with substantial traction. Levenza has signed over 300 customers, including Oliver Wyman, Kearney, Goodwin, Baird, Hg Capital and Spencer Stuart. It has secured multiple million-dollar enterprise contracts and grown profitably without raising outside capital. Customers keep expanding after they sign: Levenza’s net revenue retention is 170%, and its gross revenue retention is 99%. More than 95% of professionals using Levenza rate it highly, and many report feeling happier and less stressed at work.

"I’ve used several AI scheduling tools and Levenza stands out, as it's the first AI scheduling tool that fits how I already work,” said Dustin Finer, Managing Director of Administration at Goodwin. "It handles quick one-on-ones and more complex meetings with ease, coordinating across calendars and time zones seamlessly. Plus, Levenza lives in our existing environment, so there was no new platform to adopt.”

Levenza: one platform, for every employee, to handle every admin workflow.

Acquiring Fluid Inference

Levenza acquired Fluid Inference in September to accelerate its vision of an AI agent that people can talk to as naturally as another person. The research lab builds open-source models that hear, see, decide and speak, including FluidAudio, a #1 trending GitHub project. Its speech and system one models have been downloaded more than 4.7 million times and are used in more than 60 apps, including FluidVoice, VoiceInk and Spokenly. Fluid Inference was also a launch partner for NVIDIA's Nemotron speech models and has worked with Intel to bring speech and language models to AI PCs. Its founder, Brandon Weng, has joined Levenza as Head of Engineering.

The companies have already integrated voice into Levenza's platform. Someone driving to work can call their agent for a briefing on the day ahead, work through urgent emails and rearrange meetings without opening a laptop. Levenza users can also dictate directly into other applications. Voice is part of a broader ambition to make interacting with enterprise software less dependent on navigating applications and typing instructions.

Bringing personal agents into the enterprise

While consumer agents have demonstrated how powerful personal AI can be, enterprise environments are considerably more complex: calendars are busy and constantly changing, hierarchies decide whose time comes first, many requests route through executive assistants and every region and department works its own way. Levenza is built for that complexity. Its forward-deployed engineers work directly with customers to adapt the agent to how each firm operates, so a professional can ask Levenza in Teams or Slack to arrange a client meeting and have it inspect calendars, coordinate with assistants, resolve conflicts and book the time.

Levenza serves professionals without dedicated administrative support, as well as the executive assistants already carrying the most complex workloads. Users report saving up to three hours a day. Travel booking and expenses launch in 2027, widening the amount of admin work professionals can hand over.

The founding journey

Levenza was born from Mansour’s experience working long hours at Bain, where she saw firsthand how much time consultants and executive assistants lost to routine coordination. A UC Berkeley PhD, she founded the company two and a half years ago with Austin Tackaberry, a former Databricks and Uber engineer.

The company has grown quickly via word of mouth among large enterprises. Levenza has financed its growth through customer revenue, building a profitable business before its broader market launch.

The launch comes as companies face growing pressure to demonstrate measurable returns from their AI investments. An October Gartner survey of more than 2,000 CIOs found that just 13% said their organizations had realized significant value from AI. # Tenstorrent and ConfidentialMind Partner to Deliver Sovereign AI on Open Hardware

November 23, 2026 -

The two companies validated ConfidentialMind’s self-hosted AI platform on Tenstorrent Galaxy and will sell it across Europe, the Middle East, Asia-Pacific, and the Americas

Tenstorrent and ConfidentialMind have partnered to bring ConfidentialMind’s self-hosted AI platform to Tenstorrent Galaxy Blackhole systems. The two companies will sell the combined stack together across Europe, the Middle East, Asia-Pacific, and the Americas.

The partnership will focus on organizations that require control of their data and AI infrastructure, including governments, universities, regulated enterprises, and inference providers. Today, teams have to build a platform themselves, including inference serving, vector databases, access control, accelerator management, and observability. ConfidentialMind supplies that layer, and Tenstorrent supplies the silicon underneath it.

“Customers want AI capacity they own outright, and Tenstorrent Galaxy gives them an open system to run it on,” said Grant Jensen, Head of Software Partner Ecosystem at Tenstorrent. “ConfidentialMind supplies the deployment and management layer on top of it, so teams can stand up LLMs, RAG, and agents in their own data centers without having to build the platform first.”

ConfidentialMind validated its platform on Tenstorrent Galaxy Blackhole. The 6U server holds 32 Blackhole Tensix Processors, and customers can either run one system or scale out to a supercluster in their own data center. From a self-serve portal, customers can deploy open-source LLMs, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and agents, which the platform serves as OpenAI-compatible API endpoints. The platform also handles multi-tenancy, data connectors, accelerator management, observability, and compliance logging.

“Our customers run AI on their own infrastructure because their data has to stay there,” said Severi Tikkala, Co-Founder and GM for North America at ConfidentialMind. “Running on Tenstorrent means they are not locked in at the hardware layer either — open models, open silicon, and a platform they operate themselves.”

Tenstorrent provides the silicon, the systems, and regional field teams, while ConfidentialMind brings existing deployments across Europe, including the University of Helsinki, LUT University, Centria University of Applied Sciences, and Elastx.

About ConfidentialMind

ConfidentialMind is a software platform for deploying generative AI applications and agents inside your own environment. Founded in 2023 and headquartered in Espoo, Finland, with an office in San Francisco, the company serves enterprises, public-sector organizations, universities, and hosting providers.

About Tenstorrent

Tenstorrent is an AI compute company led by CEO Jim Keller, architect of Apple A4/A5, AMD Zen, and Tesla’s Full Self-Driving chip. Tenstorrent builds RISC-V-based AI processors and systems for developers, enterprises, and sovereign infrastructure worldwide. In addition to servers and workstations, Tenstorrent licenses its Ascalon RISC-V CPU and Tensix AI cores to chip designers including Samsung and LG. Tenstorrent’s investors include Bezos Expeditions, Samsung, LG Electronics, Hyundai Motor Group, Fidelity Management and Research Company, and others. The company operates from Santa Clara, Austin, Toronto, Belgrade, Tokyo, and Bangalore. tenstorrent.com

cross_cutting.content:
# Industry Updates

### 'SAMENA Daily' - News

#### Cassava Technologies, Mauritius Telecom partner to expand AI services across Africa

Cassava Technologies, a global technology company of African heritage, and Mauritius Telecom (MT) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) at Africa Tech Festival to develop a strategic partnership focused on strengthening compute and model access for MT’s AI services and exploring opportunities for myt Learn, MT’s AI-powered education platform, in South Africa and other African markets.

Cassava’s NVIDIA-powered AI Factory in Cape Town is Africa’s most powerful supercomputer. The partnership combines this computing scale, Cassava’s AI platforms and regional reach with MT’s own AI products, local language capabilities and operating experience.

The companies will explore access to Cassava’s AI Factory as an additional source of on-demand computing capacity for MT’s AI offerings, alongside access to AI models through CAIMEx, Cassava’s AI platform. Cassava capacity and model access would be used only for workloads where customers permit it. These options would complement MT’s existing myt AI Cloud platform and infrastructure in Mauritius and could support its expansion into other African markets.

In education, the partners will jointly assess opportunities for myt Learn, starting with South Africa’s public and private education sectors, with potential expansion into other Cassava markets. Created by MT and rolling out in Mauritian schools for selected grades, myt Learn provides curriculum-aligned guided lessons, a multilingual AI tutor and personalised revision. Teachers have access to performance insights and AI tools for marking, test creation and lesson preparation. The platform can be adapted to local curricula and teaching needs.

Together, the companies aim to demonstrate how telecommunications operators can bring locally relevant AI services to customers and take African-developed products into new markets.

Ziaad Suleman, SVP Cassava Technologies for South Africa and Botswana:

Realising AI’s promise in Africa requires more than potential; it takes infrastructure, technology, and proven expertise. By pairing Mauritius Telecom’s AI products and operating experience with Cassava’s AI infrastructure and reach, we aim to bring locally relevant AI services and education solutions to more African markets.

Veemal Gungadin, CEO of Mauritius Telecom:

We are building AI capability in Mauritius that can also serve other African markets. With myt Learn, we are already putting that capability to work in our schools, supporting both students and teachers. This partnership brings together products we have developed and Cassava’s infrastructure and reach to take that work further. Our ambition is to make trusted AI useful and accessible, while ensuring that those responsible for its use retain meaningful control.

# Deutsche Telekom and Mistral Join Forces to Advance Sovereign AI in Germany

Deutsche Telekom is strengthening its position in Europe’s sovereign artificial intelligence (AI) market through a EUR 100 million investment in French AI company Mistral. The investment, made by T.Capital Tech Fund as part of Mistral’s Series D funding round, marks the first step toward a strategic partnership aimed at bringing European AI technologies to German businesses and public institutions.

As Deutsche Telekom’s strategic investment arm, T.Capital manages more than EUR 2 billion in assets on behalf of the Group, investing in companies that support its strategic priorities. The investment in Mistral intends to combine Deutsche Telekom’s sovereign infrastructure, customer relationships, and integration expertise with Mistral’s frontier models, enterprise software, and deployment capabilities.

Through the planned collaboration, the companies aim to help German organizations adopt AI solutions tailored to their operational needs, particularly in industrial and regulated sectors. The initiative builds on Deutsche Telekom’s investments in sovereign AI infrastructure in Germany and Mistral’s growing presence in the country, including its recently established Munich hub.

Both companies share the ambition of strengthening Europe’s position in the global AI market by supporting a competitive and sovereign ecosystem spanning AI infrastructure, models, and enterprise applications.

Ferri Abolhassan, Member of the Board of Management of Deutsche Telekom AG and CEO of T-Systems International GmbH, emphasized:

Europe’s competitiveness depends on our ability to develop and use powerful AI. Businesses must be able to trust this technology while retaining control over their data. Our Industrial AI Cloud provides a strong foundation for sovereign AI in Germany. With the investment in Mistral, we are expanding the combination of frontier European AI technology and engineering expertise with trusted infrastructure and integration capabilities to help businesses across Germany put trusted AI to work.

Johan Bergqvist, Chief Financial Officer at Mistral, highlighted:

Germany is known as the industrial backbone of Europe, and AI is now core to industrial competitiveness. We built Mistral so that European enterprises can deploy frontier AI they fully control, on their own data, in their own infrastructure. T.Capital’s investment is a strong signal: together, DT and Mistral can bring sovereign, trustworthy AI to German industry and public institutions at scale.

Maneesh Sharma, Partner at T.Capital Tech Fund, added:

Mistral has established itself as one of Europe’s leading AI companies, combining world-class technology with a strong focus on enterprise needs. We see significant potential for Mistral to become a global leader in enterprise AI. Our 100 million euros investment reflects our conviction in the team, technology, and market, while creating exciting opportunities with Deutsche Telekom.

# L&T’s Vyoma.AI Secures Multi-Year Deal to Deploy NVIDIA B300 GPUs at Chennai Data Centre

Vyoma.AI, an L&T Group company, through its AI infrastructure subsidiary LTN Compute, has secured a multi-year engagement with an inference infrastructure provider to deploy additional NVIDIA B300 GPUs at its Chennai Data Centre.

The infrastructure will support the provider's AI-native platform, enabling it to train, fine-tune and deploy specialised AI models for high-performance inference at commercial scale. The deployment is expected to strengthen India's AI infrastructure and support growing global demand for advanced computing capacity.

The integrated AI Factory will combine hyperscale data centre infrastructure, accelerated computing, high-performance networking, ultra-low-latency interconnects, high-throughput parallel storage and AI infrastructure operations to support demanding AI workloads.

The facility is being developed at Vyoma.AI's Chennai campus, which is envisioned as a gigawatt-scale AI infrastructure hub. Phase 1 is designed for 250 MW of capacity and is supported by 150 MVA of power infrastructure readiness, providing a foundation for future expansion.

“Artificial Intelligence is transforming industries, and AI Factories will provide the foundational infrastructure to power this transformation. This additional GPU deployment marks another significant milestone in L&T’s vision to build world-class AI infrastructure in India. Our Chennai AI Factory will deliver the scale, performance and resilience required to accelerate global AI innovation and strengthen India’s position as a leading hub for next-generation computing”, said Mr S N Subrahmanyan, Chairman & Managing Director, Larsen & Toubro.

# L&T to deploy NVIDIA B300 GPUs at Chennai data centre

Larsen & Toubro (L&T), through its AI infrastructure subsidiary LTN Compute, has entered into a multi-year engagement with an inference infrastructure provider to deploy additional NVIDIA B300 GPUs at its Chennai data centre.

The deployment will form part of a 10,000-GPU cluster and support the provider’s AI-native platform for training, fine-tuning and deploying specialised AI models for inference workloads.

The GPUs will be deployed at the Chennai campus of Vyoma.AI, an L&T Group company. The campus is being developed as an AI infrastructure hub, with Phase 1 designed for a capacity of 250 MW and supported by 150 MVA of power infrastructure readiness.

The AI Factory will comprise data centre infrastructure, computing systems, networking, interconnects, storage and infrastructure operations.

LTN Compute provides AI infrastructure services, including AI data centres, sovereign cloud platforms, Bare Metal-as-a-Service (BMaaS), GPU-as-a-Service (GPUaaS) and managed AI platforms. Its services cater to governments, enterprises, cloud providers and AI companies.

S N Subrahmanyan, Chairman and Managing Director, Larsen & Toubro, said: “This additional GPU deployment marks another significant milestone in L&T’s vision to build world-class AI infrastructure in India. Our Chennai AI Factory will deliver the scale, performance and resilience required to accelerate global AI innovation and strengthen India’s position as a leading hub for next-generation computing.”
